title: Japan's Bullet Train
sourceNote: Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ tư liệu lịch sử đường sắt cao tốc Nhật Bản.

sections.text: On the first day of October 1964, nine days before the opening of the Tokyo Olympic Games, a sleek blue-and-white train left Tokyo for Osaka. Travelling at up to 210 kilometres per hour, it covered the distance of more than five hundred kilometres in about four hours, a journey that had previously taken well over six. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen, as the new line was called, was the world's first high-speed railway, and its trains soon became known abroad as bullet trains. Six decades later, Japan's high-speed network carries hundreds of millions of passengers a year and remains a source of national pride.

The project was far from certain to succeed. In the 1950s, many experts in Japan and elsewhere believed that railways belonged to the past and that the future of transport lay with cars and aircraft. The corridor between Tokyo and Osaka, however, was home to a large part of Japan's population and industry, and the existing line was becoming dangerously overcrowded. Shinji Sogō, the president of Japanese National Railways, argued strongly for an entirely new line, while the chief engineer, Hideo Shima, brought the technical expertise needed to build it. Part of the cost was covered by a loan from the World Bank.

A crucial decision was to build a completely separate line. Japan's existing railways used a narrow gauge, the distance between the rails, which limited the speed at which trains could safely travel. The Shinkansen was built to the wider standard gauge used in much of Europe and North America, and it shared no tracks with slower trains. The line was designed with gentle curves, avoided level crossings with roads entirely, and used many tunnels and viaducts to maintain a smooth path through Japan's mountainous terrain.

Safety has been the system's most remarkable achievement. In its entire history, no passenger has been killed in a collision or derailment of a Shinkansen train. This record is particularly impressive because Japan experiences frequent earthquakes. The network uses an early warning system that detects the first, weaker vibrations of an earthquake, which travel faster than the more destructive waves that follow, and automatically cuts power to the trains so that they begin braking before the strongest shaking arrives. In 2004, a train derailed during a powerful earthquake in central Japan, but none of the passengers on board was injured.

The trains are also famous for their punctuality. According to the railway company that operates the original line, the average delay per train is typically less than a minute, including delays caused by bad weather and natural disasters. Such reliability depends on careful organisation at every stage. At the terminal stations, teams of cleaners board each train as soon as it arrives and prepare it for its next journey in a matter of minutes, turning the seats to face the direction of travel and removing every trace of litter.

The Shinkansen transformed the economic geography of Japan. Cities along the route became closer in practical terms, making it possible to travel between them for a meeting and return on the same day, and the railway competed so successfully with domestic flights that on some routes air travel declined. Critics, however, point out that the network has also concentrated economic activity in the largest cities, drawing people and businesses away from smaller towns that the trains pass through without stopping.

The success of the Shinkansen inspired other countries to build high-speed lines of their own. France opened its first line between Paris and Lyon in 1981, and networks were later built in Spain, Germany, Italy, South Korea and Taiwan. China now has by far the largest high-speed network in the world, much of it built within the last two decades. Japan, meanwhile, is constructing a new line between Tokyo and Nagoya that will use magnetic levitation, allowing trains to travel at around five hundred kilometres per hour.

Not every high-speed project has been a success. In some countries, lines have cost far more than expected or carried fewer passengers than forecast. Yet the original Shinkansen showed that, where large cities are separated by a few hundred kilometres, a fast, frequent and reliable railway can compete with both the car and the aeroplane, a lesson that many countries are still learning today.

explain.B: Đoạn B: thập niên 1950 nhiều chuyên gia cho rằng đường sắt đã lỗi thời, nhưng Sogō và Shima vẫn thúc đẩy tuyến mới → vượt qua nghi ngờ về tương lai đường sắt: {h}.
explain.C: Đoạn C: xây tuyến hoàn toàn riêng, khổ ray rộng, không dùng chung đường với tàu chậm, không có nút giao với đường bộ → xây tuyến dành riêng cho tốc độ cao: {h}.
explain.D: Đoạn D: không hành khách nào thiệt mạng vì va chạm hay trật bánh; hệ thống cảnh báo động đất sớm tự cắt điện → bảo vệ hành khách khỏi hiểm họa tự nhiên: {h}.
explain.E: Đoạn E: độ trễ trung bình dưới một phút, đội vệ sinh chuẩn bị tàu chỉ trong vài phút → sự chính xác về giờ giấc và khâu chuẩn bị: {h}.
explain.F: Đoạn F: các thành phố trên tuyến gần nhau hơn, hàng không nội địa giảm, nhưng các thị trấn nhỏ bị bỏ qua → được và mất dọc tuyến đường: {h}.
explain.G: Đoạn G: Pháp, Tây Ban Nha, Đức, Hàn Quốc, Trung Quốc… xây đường sắt cao tốc → mô hình được nhiều nước sao chép: {h}. Bài không mô tả hình dáng đầu tàu, nên không phải {i:7}.

items.q: Which international organisation lent money for the project?
items.e: Đoạn B: 'Part of the cost was covered by a loan from the World Bank' → World Bank.

items.q: What name is given to the distance between the rails?
items.e: Đoạn C: 'a narrow gauge, the distance between the rails' → gauge.

items.q: Which type of road junction was completely avoided on the new line?
items.e: Đoạn C: tuyến đường 'avoided level crossings with roads entirely' → level crossings.

items.q: What technology will the new line between Tokyo and Nagoya use?
items.e: Đoạn G: tuyến mới Tokyo–Nagoya 'will use magnetic levitation' → magnetic levitation.

items.q: Which THREE of the following are mentioned as features of the Shinkansen's safety or reliability?
options: Power to trains is cut automatically when an earthquake begins.
Trains are prepared for their next journey very quickly.
Average delays are usually under a minute.
Every train carries a doctor in case of emergencies.
Speed is reduced at night to lower the risk of accidents.
Passengers must wear seat belts during earthquakes.
Drivers are replaced by computers on the busiest routes.
items.e: Đoạn D: hệ thống cảnh báo sớm 'automatically cuts power to the trains'; đoạn E: độ trễ trung bình 'typically less than a minute' và đội vệ sinh chuẩn bị tàu 'in a matter of minutes'. Các phương án còn lại (bác sĩ, giảm tốc ban đêm, dây an toàn, máy tính thay lái) không có trong bài.
